# Proximity Sensor System

## Overview

The proximity sensor described herein provides an effective solution for detecting and locating objects within a defined two-dimensional plane. The system architecture combines optical emission and detection components with intelligent processing to achieve precise spatial localization.

## Housing and Optical Emission Components

At the core of the proximity sensor is a housing structure that serves as the mounting platform for a series of light emitters. These emitters are strategically positioned within the housing such that each projects a beam of light outward along a common detection plane. This detection plane represents the two-dimensional region within which the sensor is capable of identifying the presence and position of objects. The light emitters may be implemented using various light-emitting technologies, such as light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or laser diodes, selected based on the desired characteristics of beam divergence, intensity, and wavelength suitable for the sensor's intended application.

## Light Detection Components

Complementing the light emitters, the housing also contains a corresponding array of light detectors. These detectors are mounted within the housing in such a manner that they are capable of sensing light entering along the same detection plane utilized by the emitters. When an object is present within the detection plane, light emitted from the emitters interacts with the object—typically through scattering or reflection—and a portion of this light is redirected back into the housing, where it can be captured by the detectors. The detectors thus serve as the sensory mechanism for identifying the presence of light returning from objects within the monitored plane.

## Emitter-Detector Pairing and Target Positions

A defining feature of this proximity sensor design is the establishment of specific emitter-detector pairs, each of which is associated with a particular target position within the detection plane. This pairing arrangement is configured such that when an object is located at or near a given target position, the light emitted by the corresponding emitter is scattered by the object in a manner that results in the maximum possible amount of that scattered light being captured by its paired detector. In other words, each emitter-detector pair is optically tuned or geometrically arranged so that its detection response peaks when an object occupies its associated target position. This one-to-one correspondence between emitter-detector pairs and discrete target positions forms the foundational basis for the sensor's spatial resolution capabilities.

## Processor-Controlled Synchronous Operation

The proximity sensor incorporates a processor that governs the operational sequence of the emitter-detector pairs. Specifically, the processor is configured to synchronously activate each emitter-detector pair, meaning that the emitter is energized to project light at the same time that its paired detector is enabled to sense any returning light. Following activation, the processor reads out the corresponding amount of light detected by each detector. This synchronous activation and readout process may be performed sequentially across all emitter-detector pairs, or through other suitable scanning schemes, to build a comprehensive picture of the light detection amounts across the entire array.

## Object Localization Through Detection-Location Relationships

Beyond simply identifying which target position corresponds to the peak detection signal, the processor is further configured to calculate a more precise location of the object within the detection plane. This is accomplished through the application of a detection-location relationship—an algorithmic or mathematical mapping that correlates the pattern of detected light amounts across multiple emitter-detector pairs to specific positions within the detection plane. 

Notably, this relationship extends beyond the discrete target positions themselves, enabling the processor to interpolate and determine object locations that lie between two or more neighboring target positions. By analyzing the relative amounts of light detected by adjacent emitter-detector pairs, the processor can estimate a more granular, continuous position for the object rather than being limited to the resolution defined by the discrete target positions alone. This interpolation capability significantly enhances the spatial resolution and accuracy of the proximity sensor, allowing it to provide fine-grained positional data even when using a relatively sparse arrangement of discrete emitter-detector pairs.

# Proximity Sensor with Interpolated Position Detection

## Field of the Invention

The present disclosure relates generally to proximity sensing systems, and more particularly to optical proximity sensors capable of determining object position with resolution finer than the physical spacing of their constituent emitter-detector elements.

## Background

Conventional proximity sensors typically employ discrete emitter-detector pairs arranged at fixed positions within a housing. Each emitter, when activated, projects light toward a target region, and light scattered back from an object present in that region is captured by an associated detector. In traditional designs, the spatial resolution of such sensors is fundamentally limited by the physical density of emitter-detector pairs—that is, the sensor can only distinguish between object positions that correspond to discrete pair locations, with no capability to resolve object positions between these discrete points.

This limitation presents significant challenges in applications requiring fine-grained position sensing, such as touchless user interfaces, gesture recognition systems, and precision object tracking, where the cost and complexity of adding additional physical emitter-detector pairs to improve resolution can be prohibitive.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses these limitations by providing a proximity sensor architecture that achieves sub-pair spatial resolution through computational interpolation, rather than through increased physical component density alone.

### Sensor Architecture

The proximity sensor comprises a housing containing a plurality of light emitters and corresponding light detectors. These components are arranged such that each emitter-detector pair is associated with a specific target position—a spatial location at which light emitted from that particular emitter is maximally scattered back toward its paired detector when an object is present at that position. This arrangement establishes a set of discrete "native" detection positions corresponding to the physical layout of the emitter-detector pairs.

### Processor and Synchronous Activation

A processor operably coupled to the emitters and detectors is configured to synchronously activate the emitter-detector pairs according to a predetermined or dynamically determined sequence. During activation of each pair, the processor reads the resulting light measurement from the corresponding detector, capturing the intensity of light scattered back toward the detector. This process may be repeated across all emitter-detector pairs within the housing, yielding a set of light intensity measurements corresponding to the various target positions.

### Interpolation Between Discrete Target Positions

The key inventive aspect of the disclosed sensor lies in the processor's capability to determine object positions that fall between the discrete target positions defined by the physical emitter-detector pairs. Rather than being limited to reporting object presence solely at the native target positions, the processor utilizes a detection-location relationship—which may take the form of a mathematical function, a calibrated lookup table, an interpolation algorithm, or a trained model—to calculate an estimated object position based on the relative magnitudes of light measurements obtained from two or more neighboring emitter-detector pairs.

For example, when an object is positioned between two adjacent target positions, both corresponding emitter-detector pairs may register partial scattered light returns, with the relative intensity ratio between the two measurements correlating to the object's precise position along the axis connecting the two target positions. The processor applies the detection-location relationship to this ratio (or to a more complex combination of multiple measurements) to compute an interpolated position estimate that lies between the discrete native positions.

This detection-location relationship may be derived through empirical calibration, in which known object positions between target positions are correlated with resulting detector measurements to establish a mapping function, or through analytical modeling of the light propagation and scattering characteristics of the sensor geometry. In some embodiments, the relationship may account for nonlinearities in scattering intensity as a function of position, as well as environmental factors such as ambient light conditions or surface reflectivity of the detected object.

### Advantages

By enabling the calculation of object positions between the discrete target positions established by the physical arrangement of emitter-detector pairs, the disclosed sensor achieves an effective spatial resolution that exceeds what would otherwise be dictated by the number and spacing of physical components. This provides several advantages over conventional designs, including reduced component count and cost for a given desired resolution, decreased power consumption due to fewer required emitters and detectors, and simplified manufacturing, while still delivering fine-grained position sensing suitable for demanding applications.

## Detailed Description of Exemplary Embodiments

In one exemplary embodiment, the housing includes a linear array of emitter-detector pairs, each pair positioned at a regular interval along the housing's length. Each emitter is paired with a corresponding detector such that light emitted from the emitter, when reflected by an object located at the pair's designated target position, is directed with maximal intensity back to that same detector. Emitters at adjacent pairs may be angled or otherwise configured such that their maximal scatter-back positions do not overlap, ensuring that each pair's target position is spatially distinct.

The processor, which may comprise a microcontroller, application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), or other suitable computing hardware, is programmed to cycle through the emitter-detector pairs in a synchronized manner, activating each emitter for a brief interval while simultaneously sampling the output of its paired detector. This synchronous activation may be performed sequentially across all pairs, or in a subset thereof, depending on the desired scan rate and power budget of the application.

Upon collecting the set of detector measurements from a scan cycle, the processor analyzes the measurements to identify one or more pairs exhibiting significant scattered light return, indicating the likely presence of an object in the vicinity of the corresponding target positions. Where a single pair exhibits a dominant signal, the processor may report the object position as coincident with that pair's target position. However, where two or more neighboring pairs exhibit comparable or partial signals, the processor invokes the detection-location relationship to interpolate the object's position between the target positions of the contributing pairs.

In some embodiments, the detection-location relationship comprises a ratiometric formula that computes the interpolated position as a weighted average of the neighboring target positions, weighted according to the relative signal strengths detected at each corresponding detector. In other embodiments, the relationship may be embodied as a lookup table populated with calibration data collected during a manufacturing or configuration process, wherein known object positions are systematically swept between target positions and the resulting detector measurements are recorded to build an accurate mapping between signal ratios and object positions.

Additional embodiments may extend this interpolation approach to two-dimensional or three-dimensional emitter-detector arrangements, wherein the processor calculates interpolated positions not only along a single axis but across a plane or volume, using detection-location relationships that account for measurements from three or more neighboring emitter-detector pairs simultaneously.

## Conclusion

The proximity sensor described herein represents a significant advancement over conventional discrete-position sensing architectures by leveraging computational interpolation to achieve enhanced spatial resolution without a corresponding increase in physical component density. Through the synchronous activation of emitter-detector pairs and the application of a detection-location relationship to interpolate object positions between discrete target locations, the disclosed invention enables cost-effective, power-efficient, and precise proximity sensing suitable for a wide range of applications, including consumer electronics, industrial automation, and human-machine interface systems.

# Proximity Sensors: Detecting Presence Without Contact

A proximity sensor is a device capable of detecting the presence or absence of nearby objects without requiring physical contact. These sensors emit an electromagnetic field, light beam, or sound wave and analyze changes in the returning signal to determine whether an object is within range. This contactless detection method makes proximity sensors valuable across numerous industries, from consumer electronics to industrial automation.

## How Proximity Sensors Work

Most proximity sensors operate by emitting a signal—whether infrared light, ultrasonic waves, or an electromagnetic field—and measuring how that signal is affected by nearby objects. When an object enters the sensor's detection zone, it either reflects the emitted signal back to a receiver or disrupts the field being monitored. The sensor's internal circuitry then processes this change and triggers an appropriate response, such as sending a signal to a control system or activating a switch.

## Common Types of Proximity Sensors

**Inductive proximity sensors** detect metallic objects by generating an electromagnetic field and sensing disturbances caused by conductive materials entering that field. These are widely used in manufacturing and industrial settings for detecting metal parts on assembly lines.

**Capacitive proximity sensors** can detect both metallic and non-metallic objects, including liquids, powders, and plastics, by sensing changes in capacitance.

**Ultrasonic proximity sensors** use sound waves to detect objects, making them effective for detecting transparent or reflective surfaces that might confuse optical sensors.

**Photoelectric (optical) sensors** rely on light beams, often infrared, to detect the presence of objects by measuring interruptions or reflections of the light source.

## Applications

Proximity sensors have become essential components in modern technology. In smartphones, they detect when a device is held close to the ear during calls, automatically disabling the touchscreen to prevent accidental input. In automotive applications, they assist with parking sensors, collision avoidance systems, and keyless entry mechanisms.

Industrial automation relies heavily on proximity sensors for quality control, object counting, and positioning tasks. Robotics applications use them for obstacle detection and navigation, while security systems employ them to detect unauthorized movement or entry.

## Conclusion

The versatility and reliability of proximity sensors have made them indispensable in countless applications. As technology continues to advance, these sensors are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering greater precision, faster response times, and integration with smart systems—further expanding their role in our increasingly automated world.

counterfactuals.output:
# Optical Touch/Proximity Sensing System with Interpolated Position Detection

## 1. System Overview

This system determines the location of an object (finger, stylus, or reflective target) within a sensing region by using an array of discrete emitter-detector pairs, each associated with a fixed, known "target position" in the coordinate space of the sensing surface. Rather than relying purely on binary detection (object present/absent at a fixed point), the processor uses the relative signal strengths from neighboring emitter-detector pairs to interpolate a continuous-valued position estimate that lies *between* the discrete target positions, achieving spatial resolution finer than the physical pitch of the sensor array.

## 2. Hardware Architecture

### 2.1 Emitter-Detector Pair Configuration

- **Emitters**: Typically infrared LEDs (850–950 nm) arranged in a linear array, grid, or perimeter configuration around or beneath the sensing surface.
- **Detectors**: Photodiodes or phototransistors, each optically and/or geometrically paired with one or more emitters.
- **Target Position Assignment**: Each emitter-detector pair is calibrated to have a specific "target position" — a defined (x, y) coordinate (or angular position, in curved/cylindrical implementations) that represents the point in space where that pair's sensitivity is maximized. This may correspond to:
  - The physical midpoint between the emitter and its paired detector (for retro-reflective or beam-break configurations)
  - The geometric intersection of an emitter's beam path and a detector's field of view (in crossed-beam or triangulation configurations)
  - A calibrated point of maximum reflected signal in reflective proximity sensing

### 2.2 Optical Path Configurations

Several physical arrangements are compatible with this architecture:

1. **Beam-break/transmissive**: Emitters and detectors face each other across the sensing plane; an object interrupts the direct light path. Target position = point along the beam path, often the midpoint.
2. **Reflective proximity**: Emitters and detectors are co-located or adjacent, facing outward/upward; an object reflects light back to the detector. Target position = the point in space (height and lateral offset) where reflected signal is maximized, determined by beam angle and detector acceptance cone.
3. **Crossed/triangulated beams**: Multiple emitters' beams intersect multiple detectors' fields of view at distinct points, creating a grid of target positions from a smaller number of physical components (N emitters × M detectors → up to N×M target positions).

### 2.3 Signal Chain

- **Emitter driver**: Sequentially or code-multiplexed (time-division, frequency-division, or CDMA-style pseudorandom coding) activation of emitters to avoid crosstalk between adjacent pairs.
- **Detector front-end**: Transimpedance amplifier converting photocurrent to voltage, followed by band-pass filtering (matched to emitter modulation frequency) to reject ambient light (sunlight, room lighting) and cross-channel interference.
- **ADC**: Digitizes each detector's response per emitter activation cycle, producing a matrix of signal amplitudes S(i,j) for emitter i, detector j (or simplified to S(k) for k designated pairs if pairs are fixed rather than fully crossed).

## 3. Signal Model

For a given active pair (or scan cycle exciting all pairs sequentially), the detector output is a function of the object's actual position relative to that pair's target position and its distance/height above the sensing plane:

```
S(k) = A(k) · f(d(k)) · g(z) + N(k)
```

Where:
- `A(k)` = baseline gain/reflectivity calibration coefficient for pair k
- `d(k)` = lateral distance between the object's true position and pair k's target position
- `f(d)` = spatial response function (typically Gaussian-like or triangular falloff, determined by beam divergence and detector acceptance angle)
- `g(z)` = attenuation as a function of object height/distance from the sensing plane (relevant in proximity sensing)
- `N(k)` = noise (ambient light residual, electronic noise, crosstalk)

Because `f(d)` is not a delta function — adjacent pairs' spatial response functions overlap — an object positioned between two target positions produces measurable signal on *both* neighboring pairs, with relative amplitudes encoding the sub-pitch position.

## 4. Processing Pipeline

### 4.1 Data Acquisition
- Emitters are strobed in a defined sequence (e.g., round-robin or Gray-coded activation) at a scan rate sufficient for the target report rate (typically 60–200 Hz for touch applications).
- Detector responses are synchronously sampled and stored as a signal vector/matrix per frame.

### 4.2 Baseline Subtraction & Normalization
- A stored baseline (no-object) signal is subtracted from each channel to isolate the object-induced response, compensating for ambient light and fixed-pattern offsets.
- Optional normalization by each pair's calibrated gain `A(k)` to equalize sensitivity variations across the array (manufacturing tolerance, LED aging, dust attenuation).

### 4.3 Candidate Region Detection
- The processor scans the normalized signal vector to identify local maxima or clusters of pairs with signal exceeding a noise-floor threshold.
- Each cluster corresponds to one candidate object; multi-touch implementations track multiple simultaneous clusters with a blob-labeling or peak-finding algorithm.

### 4.4 Interpolation Algorithms

Given a cluster of active pairs surrounding a peak, the processor computes a refined position estimate using one of the following methods:

**a) Centroid (Center-of-Mass) Interpolation**

For pairs with target positions `P(k)` and signal amplitudes `S(k)`:

```
Position_estimate = Σ [S(k) · P(k)] / Σ S(k)
```

summed over the local window of pairs (typically the peak and its immediate neighbors, or all pairs above threshold).

**b) Parabolic (Quadratic) Peak Interpolation**

Using the peak pair (index 0) and its two immediate neighbors (-1, +1) along one axis:

```
δ = 0.5 · (S(-1) − S(+1)) / (S(-1) − 2·S(0) + S(+1))
Position_estimate = P(0) + δ · pitch
```

This method assumes a locally parabolic signal profile and is computationally cheap, well-suited to real-time embedded processors.

**c) Ratiometric Two-Point Interpolation**

For configurations with sparse pairs (only two active neighbors):

```
Position_estimate = P(k) + [S(k+1) / (S(k) + S(k+1))] · (P(k+1) − P(k))
```

**d) Gaussian Fit**

For higher precision, the processor fits a Gaussian function to 3+ neighboring samples and extracts the fitted peak location — more computationally expensive but reduces bias error from asymmetric response functions.

### 4.5 Multi-Axis Extension

For 2D sensing (grid or crossed-beam arrays), interpolation is performed independently along each axis (row interpolation, then column interpolation), or jointly via 2D centroid/Gaussian fitting across the (i,j) signal matrix, yielding (x, y) coordinates. Height/proximity (z) may be separately estimated from the total integrated signal amplitude across all contributing pairs, since total reflected energy correlates with object distance.

### 4.6 Temporal Filtering
- Kalman filtering or exponential smoothing across frames reduces jitter in the interpolated position.
- Velocity-based prediction assists in tracking fast-moving objects and rejecting spurious single-frame noise spikes.

## 5. Calibration Requirements

- **Geometric calibration**: Target positions `P(k)` for each pair are determined at manufacturing time via a jig with a reference object swept across known positions, recording peak-response location per channel.
- **Gain calibration**: `A(k)` coefficients recorded to normalize LED output variation and detector responsivity variation.
- **Spatial response characterization**: `f(d)` profile is measured (or modeled) per pair to enable accurate parabolic/Gaussian interpolation coefficients, since real-world beam profiles deviate from ideal shapes near sensor array edges.

## 6. Performance Characteristics

- **Effective resolution**: Sub-pitch resolution typically 1/10 to 1/50 of the physical emitter-detector pitch, depending on SNR and interpolation method.
- **Accuracy limits**: Governed by SNR, beam profile symmetry, edge effects (fewer neighboring pairs available near array boundaries reduce interpolation accuracy), and calibration precision.
- **Latency**: Dominated by the scan cycle time (sequential strobing of N pairs) plus processing; parallel/coded multiplexing schemes reduce this.
- **Robustness considerations**: Ambient IR rejection, multi-touch discrimination (distinguishing two close objects vs. one wide object via cluster shape analysis), and immunity to partial occlusion (e.g., thin stylus vs. wide finger producing different response-width signatures usable for object-size estimation).

## 7. Typical Applications

- Infrared touch-frame overlays for displays (perimeter emitter/detector bezel)
- Proximity sensing bars (e.g., gesture strips, elevator button arrays)
- Industrial light curtains adapted for position-sensitive interruption
- Automotive interior gesture/touch surfaces
- Interactive whiteboards using edge-mounted IR arrays

# Patent Draft: Optical Detection Device with Synchronized Emitter-Detector Array

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to optical sensing systems, and more particularly to a device employing a plurality of light emitters and light detectors arranged to define a detection plane, wherein object presence and location are determined through synchronized emitter activation and analysis of received light intensity signals.

---

## BACKGROUND

Optical detection systems are employed in a variety of applications, including proximity sensing, gesture recognition, touch-sensitive interfaces, and object tracking. Conventional systems often suffer from limitations in spatial resolution, susceptibility to ambient light interference, or complexity in signal processing required to accurately localize objects within a monitored region. There exists a need for an optical detection apparatus capable of reliably determining object position within a defined plane using a coordinated arrangement of emitters and detectors, together with an efficient processing methodology.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure, an optical detection device is provided, comprising a housing; a plurality of light emitters disposed within or upon the housing and arranged along at least a portion of a periphery thereof; a plurality of light detectors disposed within or upon the housing, each detector positioned to receive light emitted from at least one of the plurality of light emitters; wherein the light emitters and light detectors are collectively arranged so as to define a detection plane extending across a region of interest; and a processor operatively coupled to the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors, the processor configured to synchronize activation of the light emitters according to a predetermined sequence, to receive signals indicative of light intensity detected by the plurality of light detectors, and to calculate a location of an object within the detection plane based at least in part on the detected light intensities.

In certain embodiments, the processor is further configured to sequentially activate individual emitters or subsets of emitters while concurrently sampling outputs from the light detectors, such that a spatial map of light intensity attenuation or interruption is generated, from which the position of an intervening object is derived.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EXEMPLARY EMBODIMENTS

### Overview of the Device Architecture

Referring generally to the drawings, there is shown an optical detection device, designated generally by reference numeral 100, comprising a housing 110 configured to support and enclose the operative optical and electronic components described herein. The housing 110 may be formed of any suitable material, including but not limited to molded polymer, metal, or composite materials, and may define a frame, bezel, panel, or other structural configuration suited to the intended application, including but not limited to touch-sensitive display overlays, security perimeter monitoring systems, industrial automation sensors, or gesture-based control interfaces.

### Light Emitters

The device 100 includes a plurality of light emitters 120a, 120b, ... 120n (collectively, "light emitters 120"), disposed at spaced-apart locations along the housing 110. In certain embodiments, the light emitters 120 comprise light-emitting diodes (LEDs), laser diodes, or other suitable solid-state emission sources, and may be configured to emit light in the visible, infrared, or near-infrared spectrum. The light emitters 120 may be arranged in a linear array, a curvilinear array, or distributed about a perimeter of the housing 110, such as along two or more edges thereof, so as to project light across a region of interest.

### Light Detectors

The device 100 further includes a plurality of light detectors 130a, 130b, ... 130n (collectively, "light detectors 130"), disposed within or upon the housing 110 at locations selected to receive light emitted by one or more corresponding light emitters 120. The light detectors 130 may comprise photodiodes, phototransistors, charge-coupled device (CCD) elements, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) photosensitive elements, or other suitable photosensitive components configured to generate an electrical signal indicative of received light intensity.

In certain embodiments, the light emitters 120 and light detectors 130 are arranged in an opposing or facing configuration, such that light emitted from a given emitter 120 traverses the region of interest and is received by a corresponding detector 130 positioned substantially opposite thereto. In other embodiments, the light emitters 120 and light detectors 130 are co-located or interspersed along a common edge or surface of the housing 110, such that light reflected or scattered by an object within the region of interest is received by the light detectors 130.

### Detection Plane

The light emitters 120 and light detectors 130 are collectively arranged such that the paths of emitted and detected light cooperatively define a detection plane 140 extending across the region of interest. The detection plane 140 may be substantially planar, or may comprise a plurality of intersecting or overlapping light paths forming a grid-like or matrix pattern, such that an object 150 intersecting the detection plane 140 interrupts, attenuates, reflects, or otherwise perturbs one or more light paths therein.

It will be appreciated that the detection plane 140 need not be strictly two-dimensional in a mathematical sense, but may possess a finite thickness or may be curved or contoured according to the arrangement of the light emitters 120 and light detectors 130 and the intended application of the device 100.

### Processor and Synchronization

The device 100 further comprises a processor 160 operatively coupled to the plurality of light emitters 120 and the plurality of light detectors 130 via suitable driving and signal-conditioning circuitry. The processor 160 may comprise a microcontroller, microprocessor, digital signal processor, field-programmable gate array (FPGA), application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), or any combination thereof, together with associated memory 170 storing instructions executable by the processor 160.

The processor 160 is configured to synchronize activation of the light emitters 120 according to a predetermined sequence, which may include, without limitation: (i) sequential activation of individual emitters 120 in a time-multiplexed manner; (ii) activation of predetermined subsets or groups of emitters 120 in a coded or patterned sequence; (iii) modulation of emitter output according to a predetermined frequency, phase, or amplitude scheme to facilitate discrimination from ambient light or crosstalk; or (iv) any combination of the foregoing.

Concurrently with, or in coordination with, activation of the light emitters 120 according to the predetermined sequence, the processor 160 is configured to sample or receive signals from the light detectors 130 indicative of the intensity of light incident thereon. The processor 160 may synchronize the timing of detector sampling with the timing of emitter activation such that the origin of detected light may be attributed to a specific emitter 120 or subset of emitters 120, thereby enabling spatial discrimination of detected light intensity variations.

### Object Location Calculation

The processor 160 is further configured to calculate a location of an object 150 within the detection plane 140 based at least in part on the light intensities detected by the plurality of light detectors 130 during the synchronized activation sequence. In certain embodiments, the processor 160 identifies one or more light paths exhibiting a change in detected intensity—whether an attenuation, interruption, or increase due to reflection or scattering—relative to a baseline or calibration value, and determines the position of the object 150 based on the identity and geometric configuration of the emitter(s) 120 and detector(s) 130 associated with the affected light path(s).

In certain embodiments, the processor 160 employs triangulation, interpolation, or a weighted centroid calculation based on the relative intensity values detected across multiple light paths to determine a location of the object 150 with a resolution finer than the physical spacing between adjacent emitters 120 or detectors 130. In other embodiments, the processor 160 may reference a lookup table, calibration matrix, or trained model correlating patterns of detected light intensity across the plurality of light detectors 130 with corresponding object locations within the detection plane 140.

The processor 160 may further be configured to determine additional characteristics of the object 150, including but not limited to a size, shape, velocity, trajectory, or number of distinct objects present within the detection plane 140, based on the pattern and temporal evolution of detected light intensities.

### Output and Communication

The device 100 may further comprise a communication interface 180 coupled to the processor 160, configured to transmit data indicative of the calculated object location to an external system, display, or control unit. The communication interface 180 may comprise a wired interface, such as a universal serial bus (USB) or serial peripheral interface (SPI) connection, or a wireless interface, such as a Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or other radio-frequency communication module.

**1.** An optical detection device, comprising:
a housing;
a plurality of light emitters disposed on or within the housing;
a plurality of light detectors disposed on or within the housing, wherein the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors are arranged to define a detection plane; and
a processor operatively coupled to the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors, the processor configured to:
 synchronize activation of the plurality of light emitters according to a predetermined sequence;
 receive signals indicative of light intensity detected by the plurality of light detectors during the predetermined sequence; and

**2.** The device of claim 1, wherein the plurality of light emitters comprises light-emitting diodes arranged along at least a portion of a perimeter of the housing.

**3.** The device of claim 1, wherein the processor is configured to synchronize activation of the plurality of light emitters by sequentially activating individual light emitters or subsets thereof in a time-multiplexed manner.

**4.** The device of claim 1, wherein the processor is configured to calculate the location of the object by identifying a change in detected light intensity relative to a baseline value for one or more light paths between the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors.

**5.** The device of claim 1, wherein the processor is further configured to calculate the location of the object using a triangulation or weighted centroid calculation based on light intensities detected across a plurality of light paths.

**6.** The device of claim 1, further comprising a communication interface coupled to the processor and configured to transmit data indicative of the calculated location of the object to an external device.

**7.** The device of claim 1, wherein the processor is further configured to determine, based on detected light intensities, at least one of a size, a velocity, a trajectory, or a number of objects within the detection plane.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how a proximity sensor could work using multiple emitter-detector pairs, each associated with a specific target position, and a processor that uses a detection-location relationship to compute where an object is located between these positions.
counterfactuals.output:
# Proximity Sensor Using Multiple Emitter-Detector Pairs

## Basic Concept

A proximity sensing system can determine object position by using an array of emitter-detector pairs, where each pair is physically associated with a specific spatial location. Rather than relying on a single continuous measurement (like time-of-flight), the system uses **spatial encoding** combined with **pattern interpretation** to localize objects, including positions *between* the discrete sensor locations.

## System Architecture

### 1. Emitter-Detector Pairs
- Multiple emitters (e.g., IR LEDs, ultrasonic transducers, or light sources) are arranged at known, fixed positions
- Each emitter is paired with a corresponding detector (photodiode, phototransistor, microphone, etc.)
- Each pair is assigned a **reference position** — the physical location it "represents"

### 2. Physical Arrangement
The pairs are typically arranged in a line, grid, or curve, such that:
- Position 1 → Emitter/Detector Pair A
- Position 2 → Emitter/Detector Pair B
- Position 3 → Emitter/Detector Pair C
- etc.

Adjacent pairs have overlapping or adjacent detection zones.

## How Position Between Sensors Is Determined

### Detection Pattern Analysis
When an object is placed **between** two reference positions, it doesn't fully occupy either sensor's zone. Instead, it partially interacts with signals from **multiple adjacent pairs**. The processor uses this partial/multi-pair activation to interpolate position through methods such as:

**A. Signal Strength Comparison (Amplitude-Based)**
- An object between positions reflects/blocks varying signal strengths at each nearby detector
- If Detector A reads 70% signal strength and Detector B reads 30%, the processor infers the object is closer to Position A, weighted proportionally
- A weighted centroid calculation can estimate the exact position:
  
  ```
  Position = Σ(Position_i × Weight_i) / Σ(Weight_i)
  ```

**B. Detection Pattern Lookup Table**
- The processor stores a **detection-location relationship** — essentially a calibrated mapping of which combination/ratio of detector signals corresponds to which physical position
- This relationship can be built empirically (calibration) or modeled mathematically (e.g., based on known emission patterns, inverse-square falloff, or beam overlap geometry)
- Given a specific signal pattern (vector of readings across all detectors), the processor looks up or computes the corresponding interpolated position

**C. Threshold/Sequential Activation**
- If binary (on/off) detectors are used instead of analog ones, the *order* and *combination* of pairs triggering can indicate position
- E.g., if Pair A and Pair B both trigger simultaneously (rather than sequentially), the object is likely between A and B
- Timing of transition from one pair's activation to the next can also hint at movement and interpolated position

## Processing Flow

1. **Emit**: All emitters activate (sequentially or simultaneously, often multiplexed to avoid interference)
2. **Detect**: Each detector reports a signal level (analog) or state (digital)
3. **Compare**: Processor compares readings from all pairs, especially neighboring ones
4. **Map**: Using the stored detection-location relationship (lookup table, formula, or trained model), the processor translates the signal pattern into an estimated position
5. **Output**: The system reports either a discrete "nearest position" or an interpolated continuous coordinate

## Example: Linear Array

Imagine 5 emitter-detector pairs spaced 10 cm apart (positions 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 cm).

| Detector | Signal (%) |
|----------|-----------|
| Pos 0    | 5%        |
| Pos 10   | 40%       |
| Pos 20   | 90%       |
| Pos 30   | 35%       |
| Pos 40   | 3%        |

The processor sees the peak at Position 20, but slight asymmetry (40% vs 35%) suggests the object is very slightly closer to Position 10 side. Using weighted interpolation, it might compute the object's true position as ~19 cm — between the discrete sensor positions.

## Key Advantages

- **Higher resolution than sensor count**: By interpolating between discrete points, the system achieves continuous position estimation without needing infinite physical sensors
- **Robustness**: Multiple overlapping pairs provide redundancy and noise immunity
- **Flexibility**: The detection-location relationship can be recalibrated for different sensor geometries, materials, or environmental conditions without changing hardware

## Summary

The system works by treating each emitter-detector pair as a **known reference point**, then using the *relative pattern* of signals across multiple pairs (not just a single reading) to mathematically interpolate an object's position — even when it lies between two physical sensor locations. This detection-location relationship, whether a lookup table or a computed formula, is the key that translates raw multi-sensor data into a precise spatial estimate.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate formal patent claim language for an optical sensing housing containing light emitters and detectors, where each pair has a maximal detection position, and a processor calculates object coordinates using interpolation between neighboring positions.
counterfactuals.output:
# PATENT CLAIMS

**Claim 1**
An optical sensing apparatus comprising:
a housing defining an interior region;
a plurality of light emitters disposed at spaced locations within or upon the housing, each light emitter configured to emit light into a detection zone associated with the housing;
a plurality of light detectors disposed at spaced locations within or upon the housing, each light detector configured to receive light emitted by at least one of the plurality of light emitters and to generate a detection signal indicative of an intensity of received light;
wherein each light emitter and each light detector responsive thereto form an emitter-detector pair, and wherein each emitter-detector pair is associated with a predetermined maximal detection position corresponding to a spatial location at which an object interacting with light from said emitter-detector pair produces a maximum detection signal for that pair;
a plurality of emitter-detector pairs arranged such that the maximal detection positions thereof are distributed across the detection zone at a plurality of neighboring positions; and
a processor communicatively coupled to the plurality of light detectors, the processor configured to:
receive detection signals from at least two emitter-detector pairs having neighboring maximal detection positions;
identify, from the received detection signals, a relative signal strength between the at least two emitter-detector pairs; and
calculate a coordinate of an object within the detection zone by interpolating between the neighboring maximal detection positions of the at least two emitter-detector pairs based on the relative signal strength.

**Claim 2**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the processor is configured to calculate the coordinate of the object by:
identifying a first emitter-detector pair having a highest detection signal magnitude among the plurality of emitter-detector pairs;
identifying at least one second emitter-detector pair having a maximal detection position neighboring the maximal detection position of the first emitter-detector pair; and
computing a weighted interpolation between the maximal detection position of the first emitter-detector pair and the maximal detection position of the at least one second emitter-detector pair, wherein weighting is based on a ratio of detection signal magnitudes of the first and second emitter-detector pairs.

**Claim 3**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors are arranged in a pattern such that the maximal detection positions of the plurality of emitter-detector pairs form a substantially uniform grid across the detection zone.

**Claim 4**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the housing comprises a plurality of walls at least partially bounding the detection zone, and wherein the plurality of light emitters and the plurality of light detectors are disposed along at least one of the plurality of walls.

**Claim 5**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein at least one light detector is configured to receive light from a plurality of the light emitters, and wherein the processor is further configured to distinguish detection signals attributable to each of the plurality of light emitters based on at least one of time-division multiplexing, frequency-division multiplexing, or code-division multiplexing.

**Claim 6**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the coordinate calculated by the processor comprises a two-dimensional coordinate within a plane substantially parallel to a surface of the detection zone.

**Claim 7**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the coordinate calculated by the processor comprises a three-dimensional coordinate corresponding to a position of the object relative to the housing.

**Claim 8**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the processor is further configured to apply a calibration factor to the detection signals prior to calculating the coordinate, the calibration factor derived from a stored calibration profile associated with each emitter-detector pair.

**Claim 9**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the interpolation performed by the processor comprises a linear interpolation between the neighboring maximal detection positions based on relative magnitudes of the detection signals.

**Claim 10**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the interpolation performed by the processor comprises a non-linear interpolation selected from the group consisting of polynomial interpolation, spline interpolation, and weighted centroid interpolation.

**Claim 11**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the plurality of light emitters comprise infrared light-emitting diodes, and wherein the plurality of light detectors comprise photodiodes configured to detect infrared light.

**Claim 12**
The apparatus of claim 1, further comprising a memory coupled to the processor, the memory storing a lookup table correlating combinations of detection signal magnitudes from neighboring emitter-detector pairs to corresponding interpolated coordinates.

**Claim 13**
The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the processor is further configured to determine, based on the calculated coordinate, at least one of a presence, a position, a gesture, or a movement trajectory of the object within the detection zone.

**Claim 14**
A method for optically sensing an object position, the method comprising:
emitting light from a plurality of light emitters disposed within a housing;
receiving, at a plurality of light detectors disposed within the housing, light reflected or interrupted by an object within a detection zone, each of the plurality of light detectors paired with at least one of the plurality of light emitters to form a plurality of emitter-detector pairs, each emitter-detector pair having an associated maximal detection position;
generating, by each of the plurality of light detectors, a detection signal indicative of a received light intensity;
identifying, by a processor, at least two emitter-detector pairs having neighboring maximal detection positions based on relative magnitudes of the detection signals; and
calculating, by the processor, a coordinate of the object by interpolating between the neighboring maximal detection positions of the identified at least two emitter-detector pairs.

**Claim 15**
The method of claim 14, wherein calculating the coordinate comprises:
determining a ratio of detection signal magnitudes between the at least two emitter-detector pairs; and
applying the ratio as a weighting factor in a linear interpolation between the neighboring maximal detection positions.

**Claim 16**
The method of claim 14, further comprising calibrating the plurality of emitter-detector pairs prior to said emitting, wherein calibrating comprises storing, in a memory, a correspondence between known object positions and detection signal profiles for each emitter-detector pair.

**Claim 17**
The method of claim 14, further comprising outputting the calculated coordinate to a display or control system for use in at least one of gesture recognition, touch detection, or proximity sensing.

**Claim 18**
A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by a processor coupled to a plurality of light detectors within an optical sensing housing, cause the processor to:
receive detection signals from a plurality of emitter-detector pairs, each emitter-detector pair comprising a light emitter and a light detector and having an associated maximal detection position;
determine at least two emitter-detector pairs having neighboring maximal detection positions and relatively high detection signal magnitudes; and
calculate a coordinate of an object by interpolating between the neighboring maximal detection positions based on the detection signal magnitudes of the at least two emitter-detector pairs.
